content.thinking:
I'll skip checking other samples and design this myself: a red panda at realistic scale—body around 0.5m, tail 0.45m, shoulder height 0.25m—standing on a mossy stone base so the model sits properly at y=0.

For the "balancing" pose, I'm thinking four legs planted on a rounded boulder with the tail arched back in an S-curve for balance, keeping it a neutral rest stance rather than anything dynamic. Stylistically I want full Genshin flair: cel-shaded fur, anime eyes, a glowing elemental motif like a dendro swirl or sprout, gold filigree details, a collar with a tassel, and mossy glowing accents on the stone itself to tie in the elemental theme.

I'm working out the boulder geometry now — building it from a deformed icosahedron with faceted shading, displacing vertices with a deterministic noise function to make it look like irregular rock, then recomputing normals so the faceting reads correctly once painted with mottled moss and stone colors.

For the skeleton, I'm deciding the stone shouldn't have its own joints, so it attaches to the root bone rather than flexing with the spine. I'm naming the root joint "root" and placing the first spine joint as its child, so the rig satisfies the expectation that the hips/pelvis correspond to the root or first spine joint, then continuing the spine chain upward from there.

Now I'm working out the rock's dimensions, trying to flatten the boulder so its top sits near y=0.20 for the panda to stand on while keeping the bottom touching the ground plane within the allowed sink tolerance.

Working out the dome height at 0.22, giving it a half-ellipsoid shape with lumpy displacement so it doesn't look like a plain hemisphere, and softening the top so it's not too pointy for a standing rock.

The bottom disc should still shade fine as a flat base. I'm also considering grouping multiple rocks together—a main boulder with smaller stones and pebbles nearby, adding moss tufts and grass on top for texture, and maybe narrowing the boulder's peak so the panda looks like it's balancing on it.

Sizing it out: a rounded mossy boulder around 0.34m wide and 0.28m tall, with the panda standing on top in a relaxed rest pose—paws spread near the edges, tail extended slightly up as a counterbalance since the rock's top is narrower than the panda's stance. I'm working through the proportions, checking shoulder-to-hip length against the rock's diameter so the overhang reads believably.

Now I'm stretching the boulder shape slightly elongated front-to-back to fully support the stance, placing hind feet toward the back edge and front feet toward the front, with the tail sweeping out behind for balance and the head facing forward for a symmetrical rest pose. I'm working out the vertical stack of heights—rock top, leg length, body axis, and head position—to get the proportions anatomically consistent.

I'm sketching the head width and ear shape, then planning the tail's bushy ringed texture, estimating an overall model height around 0.58m. Now I'm laying out the spine coordinates from hips to chest to neck to head, treating the body as a pear-shaped loft that's wider at the hips and narrower at the chest to match a rounded, fluffy red panda silhouette.

Defining joint hierarchy...

Then for the neck chain, I'm thinking parent from chest, with points for neck1 and neck2 forming a single span without a tip joint, followed by a head joint pointing forward and a jaw joint beneath it.

Now I'm working out leg placement — shoulders positioned near the chest at roughly (±0.075, 0.40, 0.14), with front foot targets near (±0.085, 0.245, 0.17), giving leg lengths around 0.075 per segment for a slight bend, matching a red panda's stout, fairly plantigrade stance using a three-segment leg chain.

I'm defining the front leg chain as shoulder-elbow-wrist-toe, with segment lengths roughly 0.07, 0.07, and a short 0.04-0.05 paw segment lying flat along the ground, named shoulderL/elbowL/wristL/pawL, with the toe serving as the chain tip and all joints assigned the "leg" role.

For the IK solve I'm using a sole constraint: the last segment stays flat, so the upper two bone lengths solve to a target offset back from the toe by the sole length, with the elbow bending backward for front legs. Hind legs get the mirrored setup -- knee bending forward, slightly longer segments (0.09, 0.085, 0.055), with hip placement and heel target height accounting for the foot's sole thickness and capsule radius.

For paw details, I'm considering dark padded feet with small toe digits and claws, but weighing whether adding four toes per foot across all four limbs fits within the joint budget.

I'm adding small claw spikes to match the semi-retractable claw look, then plotting the tail chain rising from the hips with a slight upward curve, aiming for roughly 0.45m length matching real red panda proportions.

For the tail segments I'm varying the sweep radius so it's slightly bushier mid-tail and taper at the tip, then painting alternating rust and dark rust rings along its length to create the classic banded pattern.

I'm confirming cel's lit paint resolves through the default `current` context when no s param is passed. Now picking the red panda palette: rust-red and orange-red for the body, dark brown-black for the underside and legs, and cream-white for the facial markings.

I'm also mapping the facial details -- white cheeks and muzzle, darker rust tear tracks from eye to mouth, black nose, and triangular ears with white inner tufts against dark-red outer fur. For the Genshin-style treatment, I'm layering in elemental motifs like a glowing dendro-green accent to tie the character into that aesthetic.

I'll simplify to a collar with red ribbon, gold ring, bell, and teal tassel, plus an ear cuff, using a loop around the neck for placement. For the stone, I'm adding moss clumps, glowing mushroom caps, ferns, clover, small white-pink flowers, a hanging vine with leaves, and scattered fallen leaves, while considering whether to add fur tufts on the cheeks, tail, and chest to enrich the clean cel-shaded style.

For fur texture, I'll draw card-based tufts in light neutral tones and let standard lighting shade them naturally rather than relying on tints, since baked two-tone cel shading wouldn't apply well to flat texture cards. Quality matters most here, so I'll write this carefully and plan to iterate using preview renders, starting with the head shaped as a wide, rounded sphere-like form.

Now I'm planning the head details: cheek puffs as small cream spheres, a short cream muzzle with a black nose, and a separate lower jaw with its own chin shape. For the eyes, I'm leaning toward a stylized anime look rather than the real red panda's small dark eyes -- bigger decals with an amber or green iris, probably landing on warm amber-gold with a dark pupil for a natural, expressive look.

Still planning eyebrow markings and facial shading...

Still writing paint function...

Still defining fur edge logic...

For ears, I'm thinking big triangular red panda ears with rounded tips, wide-set and angled outward, rust/dark outside and fluffy white inside — building them via extrusion of a smoothed triangular outline plus a smaller inner white face piece.

Now I'm figuring out ear joint placement and orientation: hinge-role joints "earL"/"earR" mirrored with a sign flag, tilted outward roughly 25° and forward 15°, working out the local x/y direction vectors so the extrusion thickness axis points correctly forward for each side.

Working out the mirroring math...

I'll offset the inner white layer slightly forward along the ear's local normal rather than pure world +Z, since the ears tilt forward and outward—so I need to compute the actual facing direction accounting for that tilt before placing the inner extrude.

That cross product gives the wrong orientation for the right ear, so instead I should just construct the right ear as a mirror image of the left ear's geometry across x=0, rather than trying to flip axes algebraically.

I need to work out the inner-layer offset direction for each ear, pushing slightly forward and outward using the normal derived from the mirrored axes, and account for the ear's slight outward tilt when computing the final offset vectors for left versus right.

Now I'm planning the various tuft textures I'll need—fur, moss, leaf, fern frond, grass—built as card-based SVG assets, then figuring out how to scatter cream cheek tufts around the red panda's cheek ruff, add a few tail-tip tufts, and sketch thin cream whisker rods.

I'm settling on the cel-shaded color palette: rust tones for the back and crown highlights, dark reddish-black for the chest and legs, cream for the ruff and face markings, and matching rust/dark variants for the tail stripes.

Now I'm planning the fur edge shading with gradient transitions between rust and dark belly tones, using a subtle ink outline for facial fur but leaving the belly fur soft. For the legs, I'm setting up a position-based gradient so the upper leg stays rust-colored and fades to dark near the paw.

For the stone element, I'm designing a mottled texture combining moss green patches on top with a warm gray-lavender stone base, blending noise and surface normal to determine where moss appears versus bare rock.

For the stone geometry, I'm using a low-poly icosahedron with flat shading to get a faceted rock look, and considering how the paint gets baked onto the UV atlas for that faceted surface.

Since the dome's top is uneven, I need each paw to rest at the correct height by raycasting down onto the rock surface and offsetting by the paw's radius, so the build order becomes: place the rock first as root, then compute ground contact heights for all four feet, and derive hip height from the foot height plus an offset. I'm also tuning the rock's radius and a power-curve flattening on top to create a broader plateau rather than a sharp dome.

That plateau radius comfortably fits the panda's stance, so I'll clamp ground height to zero and add small displacement bumps, lighter near the top and stronger on the sides. I should also scatter a couple smaller rocks and pebbles at the base plus moss clumps and grass-tuft cards along the plateau edges to soften the rock's silhouette.

Adding glowing dendro mushrooms near the stone base and a handful of tiny octahedron motes with sparkle cards hovering around the root joint, keeping everything within the height bound. I'm also considering a dendro rune ring etched into the stone's side for extra detail.

Now I'm placing a glowing rune decal on the front face of the rock, then thinking through color choices for a gold-trimmed teal collar with red panda warmth, adding filigree and a small bell for accent.

I'm adding a dendro-glow pendant with gem and torus ring, a small gold ear cuff with tassel, and a gold-trimmed tail band with bead charms to round out the Genshin-inspired accessories.

Now I'm figuring out how to build the body as one continuous sweep rather than seamed chains -- constructing a single catmull-rom path from hips through spine and neck to the head base, so the skin mesh stays seamless across those joints.

Working out the chain structure... I think I should build a single combined curve through hips, mid, chest, neckBase, headBase, then slice that one path into spine and neck sub-chains so they share coincident joints rather than computing separate curves that might not line up.

Now I'm defining a radius function along this path that smoothly interpolates elliptical cross-sections -- wider at hips and belly, narrowing through the chest, neck, and into the head -- using a lerp helper between control points rather than a flat per-segment radius.

I'm also figuring out where the tail root anchors into the rear of the body, placing it just behind the hip cap and parenting it to the hip joint so it inherits that motion, plus sketching how body color coating varies along the sweep -- rust on top, darker on the belly and chest, cream near the shoulders.

Now I'm layering in a mottled texture between rust and a lighter rust tone for a subtle noise-driven coat variation, then composing that through fur-edge blending at the belly and cel shading on top so the shadow colors derive automatically from each resolved base color.

For finer fur detail I'm adding cheek fur cards, dark chest tufts, and a tail tuft, skipping spine striping for now. Then I'm working out head placement in world space -- defining the skull center relative to the head joint, and setting up the ground/floor height from the rock plateau to derive spine, hip, and shoulder joint heights so the body sits correctly with the belly bottom just above the feet.

Now I'm positioning the shoulder and hip joints inward near the chest and hip surfaces, parenting the front legs to the chest-tip joint and hind legs to the hip joints, and working out foot/toe target positions by tracing from shoulder to elbow to wrist to toe along the forward direction.

I'm checking that leg segment lengths slightly exceed the vertical drop so the knees and elbows bend naturally forward, then tapering the leg radii from thick upper segments down to narrower paws, ready to sweep each limb chain with a radius function.

Now I'm setting up the paw geometry, extending the leg chain through to the toe tip and adding a flattened pad underneath plus individual toe digits as their own small capsule chains branching from the paw.

I'm figuring out the vertical placement so the foot rests properly on the rock surface, aligning the paw sole and toe centers with slightly different radii so the limb sits naturally without floating or clipping.

I'm accounting for the uneven rock top with slight height variation per foot and letting the paws sink a bit into the moss covering for a grounded look. Now I'm moving on to the head geometry: setting up the head base joint position, orientation, and the skull ellipsoid's center and radii relative to it.

Continuing with the facial features, I'm sizing and placing the muzzle ellipsoid in cream, adding a dark nose ellipsoid at the tip with a small glossy cream highlight, and setting up a separate lower jaw joint rather than a drawn mouth line.

Adding cheek radii plus ruff cards, positioning ear bases, and placing eye decals at roughly ±33° azimuth and 6° elevation on the skull. Sizing the anime-style eyes to about 0.034 by 0.046 relative to head width for a cute look, targeting the skull surface for placement.

Now I'm setting up part definitions with bone, position, scale, and direction parameters for building the tail chain—sweeping its shape with gold banding, a tip tuft, and fur cards, starting the path from the hips.

My initial waypoints made the tail too long, so I'm rescaling the curve to roughly 0.45 units, shortening each segment so the proportions better match a red panda's tail relative to the body.

I'll keep the tail centered on x for rigging neutrality rather than giving it lateral sway, with a bushy radius up to 0.07, and I'm settling on a total resting height of y0 = TOP+0.165, landing at 0.405.

Working through final proportions: tail tip reaches y=0.59, ears top out around 0.6, giving a total model height near 0.6 m, with the rock's bounding height around 0.24. For surface details, I'm scattering moss pads along the rock's top edges using a normal-based filter, flattened spheres painted in mottled moss tones, plus grass tuft textures as simple blade SVG cards with gradient green cel-shaded tones.

I'm layering in more scatter elements now: grass card clumps varying in size and lean across the rock top, mossy rounded clumps, tiny white clover flower cards, and flat round clover leaves. I'm also placing a few fern frond cards bent around the rock's base ring, and adding three glowing teal mushrooms near the east side with lathe-built caps and stems, using flat-color glow materials for the luminous caps.

Now I'm adding a hanging vine swept down from the rock's top edge with leaf cards along its length, a glowing green rune decal (rings, ticks, and a leaf-spiral glyph) on the rock's lower front, and pastel five-petal flower cards scattered near the base and top. I'm also planning dendro motes as glowing octahedron particles attached to the root bone, plus small flat-shaded gray pebble icosahedrons resting on the floor near the rock's base, making sure their lowest points clear the ground plane.

Since the model sits directly on y=0 with the stone's flat bottom there, I don't need a separate ground plate -- instead I'll add a grass ring and fallen leaf cards around the stone's base to hide the seam, along with small moss tufts. I'm checking that part and triangle counts stay well within budget, then starting to write the rock geometry function that deforms an icosahedron sphere using layered sine noise based on vertex position to create a lumpy, natural stone shape.

Still writing rock deformation logic... I'm working through how the lower hemisphere vertices collapse to y=0 to form a flat bottom disc while the upper hemisphere flares outward from the equator, making sure the noise function stays consistent across shared vertices so the surface doesn't show seams.

The icosahedron's vertices aren't exactly on the equator, so I'll just filter triangles by centroid y>0 and rebuild as non-indexed geometry with flat shading, but I need to check whether UV coordinates are needed for the part's paint/texture to work correctly.
